title: What If the Moon Fell to Earth? (Two Ways It Ends)
tags: what if the moon crashed into earth

segments.text: Right now, the Moon is 384,400 km away, racing around Earth at about 1 km every second.
segments.say: Right now, the Moon is three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres away, racing around Earth at about one kilometre every second.
segments.image: a bright full Moon rising over a calm ocean at dusk with a glowing path of moonlight on the water, vivid colours

segments.text: That speed is the only reason it doesn't fall. It is falling all the time, and always missing.
segments.image: planet Earth and the Moon seen from deep space, the Moon on its orbit with a faint curved glowing path, cinematic

segments.text: So what if the Moon came down? There are two very different ways it could happen.
segments.image: a giant Moon looming over a city skyline at night, people on the street looking up, dramatic lighting, vivid colours

segments.text: First, the slow way. Imagine the Moon spiralling in, a little closer every night.
segments.image: a huge glowing Moon low over desert mountains at twilight, much larger than normal, surreal, vivid colours

segments.text: At half its distance, it would look twice as wide and shine four times brighter. Nights would almost glow.
segments.image: a bright night landscape lit almost like day by a huge full Moon, silver fields and trees with long shadows, vivid

segments.text: But the real change is the tides. Tidal pull grows with the cube of distance.
segments.image: a coastline at low tide with boats lying on wet sand and a giant Moon in the sky, dramatic colours

segments.text: Half the distance means 8 times stronger tides. A tenth of the distance, 1,000 times.
segments.say: Half the distance means eight times stronger tides. A tenth of the distance, a thousand times.
segments.image: a towering ocean tide surging over a sea wall into a coastal town under a huge Moon, bright turquoise water, dramatic

segments.text: Coastal cities would flood twice a day, as the sea rushed in and out.
segments.image: aerial view of a flooded coastal city with water rushing between buildings, bright daylight, vivid colours

segments.text: And it's not just water. Today the ground itself rises and falls a few tens of centimetres twice a day.
segments.image: dramatic cracked rocky ground in a canyon at sunrise with warm orange light, vivid colours

segments.text: With the Moon much closer, that stretching would strain Earth's crust far more than it does today.
segments.image: a glowing volcano erupting at dusk with lava flowing down its side, bright orange, cinematic

segments.text: Then comes the strangest part. The Moon would never reach the ground in one piece.
segments.image: the Moon very close to a bright blue Earth in space, filling half the view, with thin cracks of orange light on its surface, cinematic

segments.text: Within about 10,000 to 18,000 km of Earth's centre, Earth's pull on the near side would beat the Moon's own gravity.
segments.say: Within about ten thousand to eighteen thousand kilometres of Earth's centre, Earth's pull on the near side would beat the Moon's own gravity.
segments.image: the Moon being stretched into an egg shape near planet Earth, glowing fractures, rocks lifting off its surface, cinematic

segments.text: Scientists call that line the Roche limit. Cross it slowly, and the Moon breaks into pieces.
segments.image: chunks of grey moon rock drifting apart in space above a bright blue Earth, glowing edges, cinematic

segments.text: Those pieces would spread out into a ring around Earth, just like Saturn's.
segments.image: a bright ring of rock and dust circling planet Earth seen from space, sunlit, like Saturn's rings, vivid colours

segments.text: From the ground, you'd see a glowing band arching across the sky, day and night.
segments.image: a bright glowing ring arching across a blue daytime sky above green hills and a small village, vivid colours

segments.text: Some of that rock would fall as meteors. Big ones.
segments.image: bright meteors streaking through a twilight sky over a mountain lake, fiery trails, vivid colours

segments.text: Now the fast way. Imagine the Moon simply stopped moving along its orbit.
segments.image: a giant Moon frozen in a dark blue sky above a planet, a huge clock face faintly visible behind it, surreal, cinematic

segments.text: With nothing to keep it up, it falls straight toward us. At first, slowly.
segments.image: the Moon above planet Earth in space with a straight glowing line pointing down to Earth, cinematic

segments.text: It takes about 4 days just to fall halfway. Then everything speeds up.
segments.say: It takes about four days just to fall halfway. Then everything speeds up.
segments.image: a huge orange Moon filling the evening sky above a busy city, people stopping in the street to look up, vivid colours

segments.text: The second half takes less than a day. By the Roche limit it's moving at over 6 km a second.
segments.say: The second half takes less than a day. By the Roche limit it's moving at over six kilometres a second.
segments.image: the Moon streaking toward Earth in space with a blazing trail behind it, motion blur, cinematic

segments.text: It would start to break apart, but there is no time to form a ring. The pieces keep coming.
segments.image: a cloud of huge glowing rock fragments hurtling toward a bright blue Earth, fiery edges, cinematic

segments.text: A rock a quarter as wide as Earth hitting at that speed would melt the surface. Nothing would survive.
segments.image: a gigantic fiery impact on planet Earth seen from space, glowing molten rock spreading across the surface, cinematic

segments.text: Here's the good news. The Moon is actually moving away from us, about 3.8 cm every year.
segments.say: Here's the good news. The Moon is actually moving away from us, about three point eight centimetres every year.
segments.image: astronauts' laser reflector panel on the grey lunar surface with Earth in the black sky, bright sunlight, realistic

segments.text: We know this because Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon, and we bounce lasers off them.
segments.image: a green laser beam shooting up into a starry night sky from an observatory dome, vivid colours

segments.text: And nothing we know of could stop it in its orbit. You would need to cancel a speed of a kilometre every second.
segments.image: the Moon hanging peacefully over a calm mountain lake at night with stars, vivid colours

segments.text: So which ending scares you more, the slow ring, or the fast drop? Tell me in the comments.
segments.image: a person sitting on a hilltop at night looking up at a huge bright Moon over a glowing city, vivid colours

description:
What would really happen if the Moon came down? There are two very different endings. If it drifted in slowly, it would never hit us: it would be torn apart and turn into a ring around Earth. If it simply stopped in its orbit and dropped, there would be no time for a ring.

KEY FACTS
- The Moon is on average 384,400 km away and orbits at about 1 km/s (NASA).
- Tidal pull grows with the cube of distance: half the distance, 8 times the tide.
- The solid ground already rises and falls a few tens of centimetres with the tides.
- Roche limit for the Earth-Moon pair: roughly 9,500 to 18,000 km from Earth's centre, depending on how rigid the Moon is.
- A Moon stopped in its orbit would take about 4 days to fall halfway and under a day more to reach the Roche limit, moving at over 6 km/s (our own calculation from Newton's laws).
- The Moon is moving away about 3.8 cm a year, measured with lasers bounced off Apollo mirrors (NASA Lunar Laser Ranging).

Narration is AI-generated (ElevenLabs) and the pictures are AI-generated illustrations. This is a thought experiment: the Moon is not falling.
